citizen.blurb: An AI that goes beyond answering and can actually take action.
citizen.standfirst: What actually separates an AI agent from a chatbot, how it takes real action on your behalf across several steps, and the new kind of risk that convenience carries.
citizen.core:
Ask a travel agent for advice, and they may tell you which flights are cheapest. Ask them to book the trip, and they can buy the ticket and send the confirmation. Both help, but only one finishes the job.

That is the difference between a chatbot and an AI agent. A chatbot answers and stops. An agent takes your goal and keeps working. It chooses a step, acts, checks the result, then moves to the next step. It can use tools such as search, email, or a calendar. It stops when the task is done or when it needs your help.

The key point is not the chat. An agent can take real actions for you and link several steps together without asking for approval each time.
citizen.everyday:
Say, “Book me a flight to Chicago next Friday afternoon for under $300.” A chatbot may list options. An agent can search fares, choose one that fits, enter your details, book it, and send the confirmation. It asks you only when it needs a choice that you must make.

Agents are already appearing in common tools. They can send routine email replies, fill out return forms, or find a meeting time and send an invite. That is useful, but it also means giving software access to your accounts, data, or money.
citizen.businesses:
A support agent can check an order, issue a refund when rules allow it, and follow up with the customer. A task that once took a person several minutes across several systems may now take seconds.

The risk is also higher. A chatbot may give bad advice. An agent may act on bad reasoning before anyone notices. Companies often limit what agents can do on their own. For example, a small refund may be automatic, while a larger one needs human approval.
citizen.appBuilders:
Building an agent means connecting a language model to tools outside the chat, such as search, calendars, databases, or payment systems. The model chooses a tool, reads the result, and decides what to do next. It repeats this until the task is done or a person must step in.

Much of the engineering is in the system around the model: which tools it can use, what it may do without approval, and how it handles failed steps.
citizen.modelBuilders: A good agent model needs more than conversation skills. It must follow a multi-step plan, notice when a step fails, and try another path instead of repeating the same mistake. Success is judged by whether the whole task gets done, not just whether one answer is correct.
citizen.smalltalk: A chatbot tells you what to do. An agent goes and does it, checking each step until the task is done.

technical.blurb: A language model wrapped in a loop, choosing a tool call, reading back the result, and picking the next action until a goal or stopping condition is reached.
technical.standfirst: ReAct-style free-form loops versus fixed control-flow graphs, why per-step errors compound multiplicatively across a plan, and the tool-use training and end-to-end benchmarks that actually measure whether an agent finishes the task.
technical.core:
A single-turn LLM call takes a prompt and returns text. An agent wraps that call in a loop: the model is given a goal and a set of tools, it picks an action, the action runs against the real world (a search API, a shell, a database), the result is fed back into the model's context as an observation, and the model picks the next action based on what actually happened. The loop ends when the model decides the goal is met, a step limit is hit, or a human intervenes.

The reasoning-and-acting pattern popularized as ReAct is the simplest version of this: the model interleaves "thought" tokens with tool calls, one step at a time, with no fixed plan ahead of execution. Production systems increasingly move away from that free-form version toward a fixed control-flow graph (a state machine or DAG) where the LLM is invoked only at specific nodes (plan, decide, summarize) and the transitions between them are deterministic code. The tradeoff is flexibility for reliability: a free-form loop handles novel situations better; a constrained graph fails more predictably and is easier to debug.

The mistake worth correcting here isn't "agents are just chatbots"; most practitioners already know that's wrong. It's assuming more autonomy is strictly better. Every additional step the model takes on its own is another chance to compound an earlier error, and unconstrained agents tend to fail in ways that are harder to trace than a single bad completion.
technical.appBuilders:
The core engineering surface of an agent is the harness: tool definitions with typed schemas, a memory or state store that survives across steps, retry and timeout handling for tool failures, and a permission layer that decides which actions can execute without confirmation. Frameworks like LangGraph and AutoGen give you the loop and the state graph; Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how tools and data sources are exposed to a model so the same tool definitions work across different agent runtimes.

The failure mode most worth designing against is error compounding. If each step in a plan succeeds independently with probability p, an n-step plan succeeds end-to-end with probability roughly pⁿ. At p = 0.95, a ten-step task already drops to about 60%. That math argues for keeping plans short, giving the model a way to verify its own intermediate steps (re-reading a file it just edited, checking a search result against a source), and building in checkpoints where a human or a separate verifier model reviews progress before the agent continues.
technical.businesses:
Deploying an agent changes the cost and risk profile of automation. Cost, because a single user request can now trigger a dozen model calls and tool round-trips instead of one, which shows up directly in latency and API spend. Teams typically need per-task cost budgets and step limits in addition to per-request ones. Risk, because an agent's error is an executed action, not a sentence on a screen: it sends the email, issues the refund, deletes the row. Governance shifts from reviewing the output to constraining the action space: scoped API credentials, an allowlist of permitted operations, mandatory human approval above a defined risk or dollar threshold, and an audit log of every tool call the agent made.

Observability tooling built for single-turn LLM calls (log the prompt, log the completion) doesn't capture this well. Tracing an agent means capturing the full sequence of tool calls, intermediate observations, and branch decisions, which is why agent-specific tracing tools (LangSmith, Anthropic's own tracing, OpenTelemetry-based LLM tracing) have become a separate tooling category built specifically for multi-step traces.
technical.modelBuilders: Training a model to act well as an agent generally means moving beyond next-token prediction on static text toward objectives tied to task completion. Approaches include fine-tuning on tool-use traces (examples of correct function calls and their outcomes) and reinforcement learning driven by outcomes from an actual environment: did the code run, did the test pass, did the booking succeed. That differs from learning purely from a preference judgment on a single response. Evaluation follows the same shift: benchmarks like SWE-bench (real GitHub issues, scored on whether the generated patch actually fixes the bug) and WebArena (scored on whether a simulated web task was completed) measure whether the entire multi-step task actually finished. A model can look strong on standard instruction-following benchmarks and still fail as an agent if it can't recover from a tool returning something unexpected.
technical.smalltalk: Normal LLM call in, text out. Agent: model decides an action, a tool actually does it, the model sees what happened and decides the next one, looping until the goal is actually finished.
